section: Step 0: Choose one or two Visualizations to Recreate
text:
Step 0: Choose one or two Visualizations to Recreate

Browse the set of provided visualizations and datasets
  
.Each vis is accompanied by the dataset used to create it. Select one or two visualizations to attempt to recreate.

Familiarize yourself with the dataset and its structure. Do some exploring on the Data to Viz 
  
 site to learn common vis names, caveats, and some tips to create them. As a hint, I have put the chart name in brackets for each image (though sometimes names will differ!)

Decide whether you will use AI or not – if you use it, be sure to include the link in your submission

Next, load and prepare the dataset.






Note



The dataset may require preprocessing (e.g., filtering, cleaning, or restructuring) to match the visual representation in the original image. You should document any changes you make to the dataset to recreate the visualization. You can add auxiliary data as needed, but don’t forget to cite and document it!








TipFAQs




 Do we have to write code to stream the data from the Google Docs link? 



Write some code to recreate the visualization(s) as accurately as you can






TipFAQs




 Do I need to try and replicate even the little icons and shapes? 
 Do we have to match the colors too? 
 What if I can’t get an exact 1:1 replica?



Write a step-by-step breakdown of how you created each visualization (for eample, any data cleaning or transformation required, how to change the formatting to match the original, how to add text and/or annotations, etc.).
You can do this by choosing one or more of these options:

(preferred option) Interspersing markdown cells with your code cells in notebook environments, such as Colab, Jupyter, Observable, R, Matlab. Also export to .pdf if possible.

Use Quarto to intersperse text and code (node you’ll still need to upload the runnable code)

Including block comments in your code, and line comments as well (ok option, but gets hard to read fast)

Screenshotting code snippets and putting them into a word doc interspersed with text (not recommended, but you do you)

Narrating a screen-capture video of you writing the code while explaining what you’re doing. Be sure to include closed captions/subtitles (great choice if you don’t like fiddling with documents)

Your documentation should be clear enough that another student could follow your steps and recreate your visualization without prior knowledge of the data or tool.






TipFAQs




 If I choose the video option, can I use AI to generate the narration? 
 How beautiful does my code need to be?

title: Assignment 1 Instructions
section: Step 2: Add a descriptive caption to your vis
text:
Step 2: Add a descriptive caption to your vis
Add a caption summarizing the visualization’s purpose and encodings. Check out this resource 
  
 for how to write great captions.

Some vis tools have built-in functionality for creating captions, others don’t. If you choose a tool that doesn’t, find a workaround, and then you can mention how annoying it was to have to do that in your reflection 😀.







Note



Captions are more than just titles! They should be able to stand alone if taken out of context, succinctly describing the main points the viewer should take away from looking at this image: What is being shown? What are the salient features? What task or analysis question can be completed or addressed by this vis?

Step 3: Reflection






Important



Please type in the Google Assignent doc provided on Blackboard, don’t copy paste from another doc, or it will get flagged as plagiarism by the system! Also pls no AI


As you’re working, take some time to reflect and write some short notes about:

Which tools did you consider, and which did you end up choosing to use, and why?

What challenges did you encounter in replicating the visualization?

Did you have to modify the dataset in any way to get the desired output?

Which features of your tool helped or hindered the recreation process (strengths/limitations)?

Are there elements of the original visualization that were difficult or impossible to replicate? If so, why?

What is one piece of advice you would give someone wanting to use this tool?

If you had to do this again, would you choose the same tool? Why or why not?

Write your reflection via Blackboard under Assignment 1 Part 2, then don’t forget to press ✨Submit ✨






TipFAQs




 Are bullets fine for my reflection, or do you want a full essay?

section: 1. Expected technical roles of each team member
text:
1. Expected technical roles of each team member
Every group must account for the 5 functional roles in some way.

Assign the baseline roles (Code Monkey, Project Manager, Technical Communictions Manager) of each member. Every team member should have 1 of these roles. You can define new ones, but use the given roles as a guide.
Decide how you will dole out the additional Auxiliary Roles (QA/QC, Resource Manager). For example, you can rotate them for each deliverable, or pick one person who will manage it for the whole project.







WarningFAQs




 Can we switch roles during the project? 
 How many code monkeys do we need?

title: Group Project Proposal + Group Charter (Phase 1)
text:
2. Scheduling

Indicate a weekly outside-class meeting time slot, during which everyone agrees they could be free to meet. You don’t need to always meet at this time, but make sure that there exists at least one weekly time in our space-time continuum that works for everyone. This is required.

Discuss whether anyone has any foreseeable schedule disruptions that might affect the team (conference travel, on-site job interviews, part/full time work, midterm exams). You don’t need to divulge your personal life circumstances, just let your team know if you anticipate being away at a certain time, and how you’ll stay on top of your work.

title: Group Project Proposal + Group Charter (Phase 1)
text:
1. Domain and Project Motivation
What is the Big Idea for your Project? What is the domain, who are your target users, and what tasks/analysis questions should they be able to complete with your project?






Tip





To determine these questions, do a quick internet search like you did for your Pitch to see what’s currently being done. You’ll have a chance to refine these ideas further. A great place to discover un-solved tasks in a vis area is to check “Future Work” sections of peer-reviewed publications.



When describing your analysis questions/tasks, be sure to use the concepts from Chapters 2 & 3 (Data Abstraction, Task Abstraction) in the textbook to write good tasks that are appropriate to the data types and dataset types you have identified. At least one of your analysis questions/tasks should require deriving new data/transforming data.

title: Group Project Proposal + Group Charter (Phase 1)
text:
2. Data
Identify one or more preliminary dataset(s) that would support the tasks you identify.






Important



Be sure to cite your dataset.



Dataset requirements
Your dataset should be rich enough to support multiple analysis tasks and meaningful visual encodings. Very simple two- or three- column tables typically only support a single chart type and do not provide enough structure for a semester-long project.
Datasets with only two attributes will not be approved unless you justify why the structure is inherently complex (e.g., network edges, text corpora, spatial geometries). You can also add auxiliary data (for example, adding spatial boundaries from a 2nd source to categorical place names in a simple 2-column dataset dataset).


Detail the types, semantics, and limitations

For each attribute you plan to use, include a description of the data type(s) and the semantics of the attributes (putting this information in a table in your doc might be good for this).







NoteReminders





Attribute semantics are the real-world meaning of that attribute. A dataset can have multiple types; which you choose is a design choice.




Additionally, mention some limitations of the dataset(s). A limitation is anything about the data that could affect the analysis or conclusions. Examples include:



Size and Access

Dataset too large to store
Can only be streamed via API


Coverage and Granularity

Only includes one country, platform, or time period

Missing certain populations or categories
Lacks geographic detail
Aggregated at too course resolution for the task


Missing or Noisy Values

Many nulls or nans
Inconsistent categories or labels


Provenance

Unknown data collection and processing methods
Insufficient or dubious documentation



If you choose from the above list, or find a different limitation, explain how this limitation might affect your user’s ability to complete the task(s).






WarningFAQs




 What counts as having “access” to the data? 
 Can we use multiple datasets?

Related work can be “related” by being similar in the What-Why-How framework (Chapter 1,2,3) in any of these ways:






TipWays that related work can be related




Same/similar domain
Same/similar dataset type/semantics (Chapter 2)
Similar tasks & target user (Chapter 3)

title: Revised Proposal + Related Works (Phase 2)
text:
Step 1: Find Inspo
Both individually and as a group, search for many related visualizations and add them to whatever tool your group is using for brainstorming.






Important



Please note that if you do get your vis from an internet compiled list (listicle) this is usually NOT the original source; you must search for the original publication/post. Typically posts on reddit say something like [OC] for original content (but not always), which would be considered the original source, but be sure to double check.
Here is an example of a listicle: https://visme.co/blog/best-data-visualizations/. Note that it has no links to the originals, which means it is a bad source and should not be used. If you really like an image you can go look for the original, but that may be a bad use of your time.



Your sources should be relevant to the visualization aspects of your project. Please take care that you are not including sources that are only relevant to the domain or non-visual analysis technique.







WarningFAQs



My source is about the same topic as my project, does that make it a valid related work?



Each person in your group must contribute at least 2 unique items to the collection, and write some quick notes in your google doc describing 1) how the source’s author(s) visually encode their data (marks, identity channels, magnitude channels), and 2)how it is similar to and/or different from your proposed approach/idea.

title: Revised Proposal + Related Works (Phase 2)
section: Step 3+: Continue to search to avoid design fixation
text:
Step 3+: Continue to search to avoid design fixation
Keep updating this collection of related work throughout your project, as features, scope, tasks, etc evolve. Prune as needed.






NoteWhat is design fixation and why should we care?



Design fixation is the tendency to get stuck on an initial concept and unconsciously constrain your thinking around it, even when better solutions exist. It’s the mental trap of anchoring too early on a specific idea, making it hard to explore genuinely different directions.
Why does it matter for this project and beyond?

A lot of times people settle on familiar vis idioms because they are familiar, not because they are the most effective for your user/task/data
It’s also easy to gravitate toward whatever the default output of a library looks like, instead of what your data and user actually need
Seeking out varied references across domains and styles forces you to decouple the design problem from the implementation

text:
Rubric
[Rubric] Phase 1
[Rubric] Related Works



  
    Check Beall's List, which is a list of potentially predatory publishers and journals. You can also look for signs like: the journal charges high fees with little editorial oversight, it accepts papers very quickly with minimal peer review, or it's not indexed in major academic databases. When in doubt, do a quick search for the journal name alongside the word "predatory" or ask the Professor.
  

  
    Your related works collection is meant to inspire your visual design, not your domain knowledge or analytical methods. A related work is relevant if the visualization technique could plausibly be applied to your dataset. This means the marks, channels, and idioms used in the source are compatible with the structure of your data: the attribute types, dataset types, and tasks involved. Topic overlap alone does not make something a valid related work.
    For example, if your dataset has two quantitative attributes and a categorical grouping, a scatterplot with color encoding is relevant. A chord diagram showing relationships between nodes is not, unless your data has that relational structure or you plan to derive the relationships.
  

  
    The listicle itself cannot be your source, you must cite the original publication or post. If you find the original, then yes, you can use it, as long as it meets the quality standards described in Part 0. Be aware that tracking down originals can be time-consuming; it may be more efficient to search for high-quality sources directly.
  

  
    Take a screenshot.
  

  
    When you paste a link directly into sites like these, the image shown is the website-defined thumbnail, which may not be the one you want. If the image isn't the right one, you can click "remove" and add a screenshot instead, and put the link in the caption. You'll also need to do this if it's a pdf of a paper.
